text:
Help me write a case for my promotion. I'm the assistant front office manager at a 180-room hotel, and the front office manager job is open. I'm applying, and my general manager wants it in writing by Friday.

Facts:
- I've worked here 6 years, the last 2 as assistant manager.
- Our guest score for check-in on the main review site went from 7.9 to 8.6 over the last 18 months. The lobby and all the rooms were renovated during the same time.
- I rewrote the front desk training. New hires now work the desk alone after 5 shifts instead of 9.
- Front desk turnover was 9 of 14 people in the year before I became assistant manager, and 5 of 14 last year.
- I've covered the front office manager's job alone for the 7 weeks since she left.
- I have never managed a budget. The front office manager owns a $1.1 million payroll budget.

I want it to say I'm the main reason our guest scores went up. One page.

Before I draft, there are two things to settle: the guest-score claim and the budget gap.

**The guest-score claim.** Your facts don't support saying you're the main reason scores went up. The lobby and every room were renovated in the same 18 months, and your GM approved that renovation. If the page credits you for a rise they know overlaps with a new lobby, they'll discount it, and they may discount the rest of the page too. That would be a waste, because the rest of your case is strong:

- Front desk turnover fell from 64% (9 of 14) to 36% (5 of 14).
- New hires now work the desk alone after 5 shifts instead of 9, which is 44% less training time per hire.
- You've already done the job alone for 7 weeks.

Here's a version your facts do support: "The check-in score rose from 7.9 to 8.6 while I rebuilt how the desk is staffed and trained. A renovation can improve a lobby, but check-in is mostly the person behind the desk." Your GM can't easily wave that away. Whether we can say more depends on question 1 below. You decide which version goes in.

**How I'd build the case.**
- **Claim:** You should be the next front office manager.
- **Grounds:** Lower turnover, faster training, 7 weeks running the department alone, 6 years at the hotel, and the check-in score rising alongside your changes.
- **The link:** The best predictor of how someone will do this job is how they've already done it, and you've been doing it.
- **Main objection:** You've never owned a budget, and this job owns $1.1M in payroll. I'll name that directly instead of leaving it for your GM to bring up.
- **Second objection:** "The renovation raised the scores."

**Questions** (most useful first):

1. **Separating your work from the renovation.** Do you have any of these?
   - Other category scores on the same review site (rooms, cleanliness). If check-in rose as much as or more than rooms, that matters a lot.
   - When the new training started compared with when the renovation finished.
   - Reviews that name desk staff.
2. **The budget.** What have you done that touches payroll? For example, building schedules, controlling overtime, approving hours or deciding staffing levels, especially in the last 7 weeks. And what would you commit to? For example, monthly payroll reviews with the controller or GM for your first 6 months. Only tell me what you'd actually stand behind.
3. **The 7 weeks.** What happened? Any numbers that held or improved, problems you handled, or anything that would have gone wrong without you?
4. **Turnover cost.** Does the hotel know roughly what it costs to hire and train one desk agent? With that, the turnover drop becomes a dollar figure, which speaks directly to the payroll concern.
5. **Your GM.** What do they already think of your work? Is anyone else in the running, inside or outside the hotel?
6. **Anything they'll find out anyway.** Is there a complaint, a missed target or a rough patch your GM knows about or will hear about? It's better to address it on the page than have it come up afterwards.

Answer whatever you can and skip the rest. I'll write the one-page version from what you give me and won't fill any gaps with guesses.

Fair point on "main reason." I'm fine with just saying what I did.

1. Renovation started 5 months into the 18 months, and check-in had already gone from 7.9 to 8.2 before it started. I don't have the other category scores or the date the training started compared with when the renovation finished. Not sure about reviews naming staff.
2. In the 7 weeks, overtime came in under the monthly plan. I'd commit to finishing the company's finance course in my first 3 months (company pays). Our controller, Ben Oduya, offered weekly sessions on the payroll budget and I'd do those.
3. No front desk shift went uncovered in the 7 weeks, and overtime was under plan.
4. Don't know.
5. GM is Mark Ellison. I don't know exactly what he thinks of my work. There's an outside candidate with experience at a larger hotel, and I can't match that.
6. Friday evening check-in waits are still the most common complaint at the desk.

I've drafted the case below. The fact that check-in reached 8.2 before the renovation started turned out to be your strongest point. Almost half the gain (0.3 of 0.7) came before any construction began. I state it as a plain fact and don't claim credit for the whole rise, so Mark can draw his own conclusion.

<final_document>
Mark,

I'm applying for the front office manager position. I've done the job alone for the past seven weeks, and I'm asking you to make it permanent.

**What I've done for the front desk**

- **Training.** I rewrote the front desk training. New hires now work the desk on their own after 5 shifts instead of 9.
- **Turnover.** In the year before I became assistant manager, 9 of our 14 front desk staff left. Last year, 5 of 14 left. Fewer people leaving means fewer new hires to train and a more experienced team at the desk.
- **Guest scores.** Our check-in score on the main review site rose from 7.9 to 8.6 over the last 18 months. The lobby and rooms were renovated during that time, so I'm not claiming the whole rise. But the score had already reached 8.2 before the renovation started.

**The last seven weeks**

Since the position opened, I've run the front office alone. No front desk shift has gone uncovered, and overtime has come in under the monthly plan.

**The budget**

I have never managed a budget, and this job owns a $1.1 million payroll budget. Here is how I'll close that gap:

- I'll finish the company's finance course within my first three months.
- Ben Oduya has offered me weekly sessions on the payroll budget, and I'll take them.
- I've already handled one part of the payroll: overtime, which has stayed under plan for the past seven weeks.

**What's still unsolved**

Friday evening check-in waits are still the most common complaint at the desk. If I get the job, fixing that is the first problem I'll take on.

**Why me over an outside candidate**

I know you're also considering a candidate who has worked at a larger hotel. I don't have that experience. What I offer is six years at this hotel. I trained most of the team now working the desk. The changes that brought turnover down and check-in scores up are mine, and I'd be there to keep them going. And I've already shown you how I run the department, because I've been running it.

Thank you for considering me. I'd welcome the chance to talk it through before you decide.
</final_document>

Before you send it:

- **Your name:** I left the signature off because I don't have your name. Add it at the end.
- **Friday evening waits:** The page commits you to making this your first project. If you already have a plan, such as staggered shifts or a second agent on Fridays, put one sentence about it there. A specific plan is stronger than a promise.
- **Other review scores:** If you can get the rooms or cleanliness scores from the review site before Friday, compare them with check-in. If check-in rose as much as those did, or more, add one line saying so. It would strengthen the guest-score point more than anything else could.
